  against each lane's TRAINING-SET mean, which this probe does not carry.
```

So the three-reference-frames concern is **still untested**. What #62 changed is that nothing now claims otherwise.

For the record, the measured between-lane displacement at `A = 0` — the data this issue predicted would exist — leans the way the issue expected: the four named lanes sit **1.86–3.57 dB below `unknown`, all the same direction, at 3.8–7.3 se**. That is consistent with an intercept shift *and* with the lanes genuinely being quieter deliveries, and the 90 existing renders cannot separate the two.

## What remains

Join each lane's `A = 0` rendered LUFS to that lane's training-set mean from `labels_v6.jsonl`. Both artifacts exist — `/data/model-training/sonora/probes/delivery_ep010/measures.csv` and the labels file — so this is a derivation, not a new render pass.

issue_comments.author: lmcfarlin
issue_comments.body:
**The test this issue asked for has been run — #73.** Reporting the result here rather than closing, because the finding is a decision for the owner and the issue's own question is only half answered.

## What was run

> **What would actually test it:** compare absolute output LUFS at `A = 0` across lanes … against the corresponding training-set means.

`scripts/derive_a_channel_stats.py` **§ 9** joins `labels_v6.jsonl` (corpus rows at |A| ≤ 0.25) to the same 90 renders. Both profiles are centred on their own named-lane mean, so the checkpoint's −7.376 dB global offset from the corpus cancels and only the between-lane shape is compared. No `unknown` term is used — `unknown` is not a lane in the corpus, which is why every earlier comparison against it was confounded.

| lane | n | train @ A≈0 | render @ A=0 | train dev | render dev | discrepancy |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Dialogue | 312 | −22.920 | −32.081 | **+0.952** | **−0.833** | −1.785 (4.4 se) |
| Neutral | 288 | −23.162 | −31.549 | +0.710 | −0.300 | −1.011 (2.4 se) |
| Newscaster | 76 | −23.009 | −30.994 | +0.863 | +0.255 | −0.608 (1.5 se) |
| Speech | 48 | −26.399 | −30.370 | **−2.526** | **+0.878** | **+3.404 (9.0 se)** |

**Spearman ρ = −0.80.** The order is nearly inverted: Speech is the corpus's quietest lane by 3.4 dB and renders as the *loudest* of the four. Training spread 3.48 dB, rendered 1.71 dB. ⚠ Insensitive to the band — ρ = −0.80 at |A| ≤ 0.10 / 0.25 / 0.50 / 1.00 / unbanded, Speech between +3.16 and +3.55 dB throughout.

## This issue's first claim is upheld

The probe measured a **slope** and was cited as falsifying an **intercept** concern. That was withdrawn on #62. The two reported gaps are also closed: every per-lane number now carries a CI, and the "pooled 0.554 dB noise floor" was neither pooled nor a floor (true pooled within-cell sd **0.7616 dB**).

## Its second inference does not survive

> the between-lane spread exceeds the stated noise floor … evidence of *lane-dependent dial gain*

The 1.18 dB slope spread is a **maximum over ten lane pairs** and was being referred to the null of one pre-specified pair. As a studentised range (k = 5, df = 75) **p = 0.434**, not 0.003. So the spread is not evidence of lane-dependent gain — the hedge already in § 3b was right and the number disagreed with it.

## ⚠ What § 9 does NOT establish

*"The named lanes are genuinely quieter deliveries"* predicts a **positive** correlation, so that reading is refuted and § 8's confound is closed. But a negative correlation is only **consistent** with the three-reference-frames mechanism, not proof of it: **"the model has not learned lane loudness at ep010" predicts the same table.** Distinguishing them needs a second checkpoint, or a re-cut with target-clustered offsets — neither is a measurement this probe can make, and § 9 prints that caveat in its own output rather than leaving it to a reader.

Limits: 4 lanes, 2 texts, 6 renders per cell, one checkpoint.

## The decision this leaves

The correct statement is now: **the dial works; `A = 0` does not mean the same thing across lanes; and the reason is not that the lanes are quieter.**

That is the condition [#14](https://github.com/Artificial-Humanity/Sonora/issues/14) pre-committed to re-cutting v6 on — *"re-cutting v6 with target-clustered offsets is its own commit"* — so whether it fires now is the owner's call, not this issue's. Left open pending that.

issue_comments.author: lmcfarlin
issue_comments.body:
**§ 10 answers the half § 9 left open: the cause is STRUCTURAL.** In #73.

§ 9 closed § 8's confound but said plainly that two readings predict its table — (a) the reference frames disagree, or (b) the model has not learned lane loudness at ep010. They differ in what *training* does, so all three checkpoints were re-probed on one design.

⚠ First, why re-rendered rather than compared against the existing probe: **`probes/delivery_ep010/` records neither its texts nor its speaker nor its sampler settings** — the script that produced it was never committed. Comparing a new checkpoint against it would confound the epoch with the stimulus. `scripts/probe_delivery_intercept.py` is that design written down, and every checkpoint below went through it.

| checkpoint | ρ | rendered spread | ÷ training spread | worst lane | worst deviation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| ep002 | −1.00 | 3.66 dB | 1.05 | Speech | +4.43 dB |
| ep008 | −0.80 | 2.19 dB | 0.63 | Speech | +3.82 dB |
| ep010 | −0.80 | 1.95 dB | 0.56 | Speech | +3.49 dB |

**The readings predict opposite trends and the data picks one.** (b) needs the rendered spread to **grow toward** the corpus's 3.48 dB with ρ rising. It **shrinks away** from it — 3.66 → 1.95 dB — while ρ stays negative throughout.

The ep002 row is the informative one: **the magnitude was already right (3.66 vs 3.48) and the order was exactly inverted (ρ = −1.00).** Training has flattened it rather than reordered it.

⇒ **The model is converging on lane-independent loudness at `A = 0`, not on the corpus's profile** — which is what a signal centred out of the labels looks like. There is nothing to learn, so the residual decays.

## ⚠ Limits, including one that closes an option

3 checkpoints, **one training run**, 4 lanes. ρ over 4 items moves only in steps of 0.2, so the spread column carries the weight — it is the continuous one. And **the run stopped at ep010 on a flat basin, so "train longer" is not something this corpus offers**: the trend cannot be extended by waiting, and a second run would be a different experiment rather than more of this one.

## What this issue now leaves

This issue's own question is answered. What remains is not this issue's to decide: **[#14](https://github.com/Artificial-Humanity/Sonora/issues/14) pre-committed to re-cutting v6 with target-clustered offsets on exactly this condition**, and whether that fires is the owner's call.

Staying open until that call is made, so the evidence and the decision are not separated.

issue_comments.author: lmcfarlin
issue_comments.body:
**Closing: the question this issue asked is answered, and the owner has ruled on what follows.**

## Answered

1. **The probe measured a slope and was cited as falsifying an intercept concern.** Upheld — that claim is retracted in `direction-contract-v3-proposal.md`, and the probe now claims dial gain only.
2. **No interval on any per-lane number.** Fixed — every figure carries a 95% CI, and the "pooled 0.554 dB noise floor" was neither pooled nor a floor (true pooled within-cell sd **0.7616 dB**).
3. **"The between-lane spread is evidence of lane-dependent dial gain."** ⚠ This inference does **not** survive. The 1.18 dB spread is a maximum over ten lane pairs and was being referred to the null of one pre-specified pair; as a studentised range (k = 5, df = 75) **p = 0.434**, not 0.003.
4. **"What would actually test it."** Run, as §§ 9–10 of `derive_a_channel_stats.py`, with the probe itself finally committed as `scripts/probe_delivery_intercept.py`.

**Result: ρ = −0.80, and the cause is structural.** The rendered between-lane loudness at `A = 0` is anti-correlated with the corpus's; across ep002 → ep008 → ep010 the rendered spread *shrinks away* from the corpus's 3.48 dB (3.66 → 1.95) while ρ stays negative — the opposite of what "hasn't learned yet" predicts. The model is converging on lane-independent loudness, which is what a signal centred out of the labels looks like.

## Ruled on

**Owner, 2026-08-12: the v6 re-cut is DECLINED, and the decline is recorded as COST rather than resolution.**

⚠ The 2026-08-11 override rested on three reasons, one being *"there is no measured inference defect to buy with that cost"*. **That leg is now false**, and it is struck in place in the note rather than deleted, so the two calls can be compared. The decline now stands on cost alone: rung 2's holdout comparability, and a selected, trained `ep008` that a re-cut would also re-run.

The debt is written down with its consequences named — `A = 0` denoting different loudness per lane (up to 3.49 dB, inverted); the delivery block carrying no loudness intercept and converging on carrying none; no resolution available on this corpus, since the run stopped at ep010 on a flat basin; and v7's `loudness_target` re-key now knowingly designed on a measured defect.

## ⚠ The honest limit, and what would reopen this

§§ 9–10 measure **the label geometry reaching inference, not what a listener hears.** The defect is established; **its audibility is not.** A measured quality or ear consequence attributable to the intercept — not to the dial, which works — is what would reopen the re-cut.

Everything above regenerates: `.venv/bin/python scripts/derive_a_channel_stats.py --probe-series ep002=… ep008=… ep010=…`.

issue_comments.body:
## 8. Guard code is written without the discipline it exists to enforce

Added 2026-08-12 after #74, #75 and #76. **This is now the highest-yield item in this issue**, because it is the one where the review lane spent most of its rounds.

### The pattern

Across those three PRs the reviewer raised **47 findings**. From round two onward, almost every one was in code written to *fix a previous round's finding* — and specifically in the **guards**, not in the product code they guard. Sixteen were the same underlying fault. It is not sixteen kinds of carelessness; it is four mechanisms:

| mechanism | n | representative instance |
|---|---|---|
| **The check could not fail** | 4 | a fixture asserting `"scripts" in out[0]` — the detector's own append condition; a coverage floor counting files *enumerated* instead of paths *asserted* |
| **Red and green could not distinguish outcomes** | 1 | a guard raising `AttributeError` while catching an evasion; pytest renders that as the same `1 failed` as a real catch, and it shipped |
| **The instrument was not what it was taken to be** | 6 | `ast.parse` for a `compile()` question (missed a `SyntaxError` on `main`); `--select=F` for a syntax error (`E999` is not an F-code); bare `flake8` vs the repo's configured args; `black --quiet` suppressing the lines being counted |
| **Verified in the wrong environment** | 1 | the lint gate passed locally because `.venv` is a *symlink* here and flake8 will not walk one; CI creates a real directory and the gate went red on `_pytest`, `cffi`, `anyio` |
| **Numbers copied instead of re-derived** | 3 | `95`→`94`, `13`→`24`, and the prose beside a floor that was re-derived while the prose was not |

**The unifying fault:** guards were verified by observing them *pass*, and the ability to fail was inferred. Nearly every instance dissolves under one discipline — *produce the failing case, in the target environment, and read the specific rejection message.*

⚠ **The cost was not theoretical.** `scripts/litert_export/convert_vat.py` — the LiteRT export converter — sat on `main` not compiling. It was introduced by a layout move, and the sweep that caught the *identical* breakage in another file the same afternoon used `ast.parse`, which structurally cannot see `return` outside a function. One broken file was reported when there were two. Nothing else noticed because nothing imports the export lane, so its first real syntax check would have happened on a GPU host, hours into a run.

### Proposal, ranked by leverage

**8a. Move the detectors out of the test files.** There are **~1,920 lines** of AST walkers and shell parsers living inside `tests/test_audit_sampling.py`, `test_stage_coverage.py` and `test_asset_paths.py`. That is why they drifted: they are not linted as code, not importable by name, not reviewable as things with a contract, and invisible to any tool that looks at "the tests". A `tests/guards/` module with its own test file makes them ordinary code. **Prerequisite for 8b and independently worth it.**

**8b. Mutation testing on the detectors — the mechanical answer to "can this check fail?"** A surviving mutant *is* a check that cannot fail. This is the automated form of what was being done by hand and done incompletely. Verified feasible: the detectors already import in isolation outside pytest. Scope to the ~10 detector functions, **not** the repo; advisory in CI first, since it is slow. ⚠ Cap it — treat a *rising* surviving-mutant count as the signal rather than chasing zero, or this becomes a rabbit hole.

**8c. A negative-control meta-test** — the cheap interim if 8b is too heavy. For every public detector, assert that at least one test asserts a **non-empty** result. Mechanically checkable, an afternoon, and it targets the "could not fail" class precisely.

**8d. For CI and workflow changes, the verification artifact is the CI run, not a local invocation.** The symlink-vs-directory failure proves nothing local can substitute. A convention rather than a mechanism, but with a natural forcing function: push, read the log, cite the run in the PR.

**8e. Stop stating counts in prose; compute them.** All three number slips were prose-versus-artifact — and this repo already owns `scripts/gates/test_doc_claims.py`, whose entire purpose is comparing documented numbers against reality. **Extend that gate to the guard docstrings** rather than inventing a second mechanism.

### What this should deliberately not be

A new AGENTS.md section as the *fix*. By §1's own rule — *"a rule in this file is not an enforcement mechanism"* — that is documentation. A pointer is worth adding **after** the mechanisms exist, not instead of them.

### Sequencing

**8a then 8b as one refactor.** 8c only if value is wanted before that lands. 8e folds into whatever next touches those docstrings.

---

## Data update to item 1 (convergence)

Item 1 was written from **one** PR (#62: 7 → 5 → 9 → 7, rate flat). Three more PRs of evidence, and it needs qualifying rather than restating:

| PR | round 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| #74 (200 files) | **24** (4 high) | 7 (1 high) | 5 (0 high) | — |
| #75 (3 files) | 7 (0 high) | — | — | — |
| #76 (14 files) | 4 (1 high) | — | — | — |

**Volume does decline** — 24 → 7 → 5 — which #62's flat 7→5→9→7 did not show. **Severity converges faster than volume**: highs went 4 → 1 → 0. So item 1's "does not converge" is too strong as stated; the accurate claim is narrower and more useful:

> A large diff produces a large first round, and the rounds after it are dominated by defects in the previous round's **fixes** rather than in the original change. Shrinking the diff is what shortens the tail — and the tail migrates from product code into whatever was written to guard it.

That last clause is what item 8 exists to address, and it is why 8 belongs in the same refactor rather than a separate pass.

issue_comments.body:
### Item 8b, run by hand on four fixes — and the case for making it standing

#77 merged with three unresolved round-3 findings; #78 fixes them. One of the three is the reason this item exists, so here is the concrete evidence rather than another restatement of the intent.

**What happened in #77:** two fixes to two separate findings landed in one commit and **cancelled each other**. Fix A added `\n` to a clause-terminator set; fix B, twelve lines away, added a `head.split()` + `" ".join(...)` normalisation that flattens newlines to spaces. Fix B ran first, so fix A never saw a newline — and fix B's caller is fix A's *only* reachable caller. The round-2 HIGH shipped **inert**, verified once by hand against the exact string in the finding, and the suite stayed green either way.

**Why per-commit verification cannot catch this.** I verified fix A (newline case → reported) and fix B (`/bin/echo` → exempt) individually as I wrote them, and both were true *at the moment I checked*. The interaction is what broke it, and nothing re-ran fix A's check after fix B landed. A commit-level "does the suite pass" tells you nothing, because neither fix had a fixture.

**What actually closes it** — revert each fix independently, confirm each goes red:

```
BASELINE                                     150 passed
M1  drop \n from _CLAUSE_END                  4 failed  -> caught
M2  drop the PATH PREFIX from _ECHO_HEAD      8 failed  -> caught
M3  is_wholly_printed -> naive .strip()       3 failed  -> caught
M4  restore head.split()/join()               2 failed  -> caught
RESTORED                                     150 passed
SURVIVORS: none
```

Two things about the harness that matter more than the result:

1. **It aborts if the anchor string isn't found.** A mutation that silently fails to apply reports "caught" for the same reason a skipped test reports green — the [4+ instrument failures](https://github.com/Artificial-Humanity/Sonora/issues/68) pattern. Earlier in this chain I compiled an empty file three times and read "compiles".
2. **It refuses to run if the baseline is red**, because mutation results against a red baseline are unreadable.

**Proposed rule, narrower than item 8 as filed:** a fix to a *guard* is not verified until the guard's own fixture fails without it. Not "add tests" — specifically, revert the fix and watch the new assertion go red. That is one command per fix and it is the only thing that would have caught the #77 collision, since the collision is invisible to any check that runs before the second fix lands.

Sequencing note: this supersedes the 8a→8b order I proposed. 8a (extract the detectors) was already done in #76/#77; 8b turns out to be the load-bearing half and does not need 8a finished first — the battery above ran against the detectors exactly as they sit today.

Also worth noting against this issue, since it is the same failure class one layer up: #78 fixes an **AGENTS.md** diagnostic that could not detect the failure it was written for. The `| grep -E '^[<>]fc'` I added in #77 to suppress rsync metadata noise silently dropped every itemisation for a file *missing* from a deployment and for a file about to be *deleted*. It was tested in the noise direction only, never in the direction of the failure it exists to catch. That is the second instrument in that one paragraph to fail that way (`test_data_mirrors` was the first). **A guard needs a fixture for the false-negative direction, not just the false-positive one** — the same rule as above, applied to prose.

issue_comments.body:
### Closing the loop on #78 — and two things for item 8 that came out of it

Owner has called `13df79d` the last change to `tests/test_audit_sampling.py` / `tests/test_stage_coverage.py` in this PR, regardless of what a further review round says. Recording what is settled, what is not, and the correction to the rule I proposed above.

#### The rule as filed is necessary and NOT sufficient

I proposed: *a guard fix is not verified until the guard's own fixture fails without it.* That is right and it caught real things — 16 mutations, no survivors, including two of my own fixes that had quietly become untested. But #78's round 3 returned **four findings, all four regressions from my own fixes in the same PR**, at a moment when the branch carried 12 mutations with no survivors, ~200 fixtures, and a 6,952-evaluation differential showing zero verdict changes on real repo lines. All of it passed. The findings were real anyway.

**A mutation battery scores the fixtures you already wrote.** It answers "is this fix tested", never "do my tests span the input space". Two additions, both earned:

1. **Ask what the new rows have in COMMON, and write the row that breaks it.** Three rounds running, my fixtures inherited the incidental shape of the finding's examples, and the miss was always outside it:
   - round 1's path rows all put the verb *at a clause start* → missed argv[0] with an **interior** segment;
   - round 2's substitution rows all put the substitution *last* → missed a substitution **before** the name;
   - round 3's launcher rows all put the whole command in *`args[0]`* → narrowing the haystack blinded **10 of 18 launchers** (`os.exec*`/`posix_spawn*`, where `args[0]` is the executable).
2. **The assertion has to be able to see the defect.** Two replacement rows I added this round survived their mutation because I asserted `is_wholly_printed` while the defect was *erasure of the script name* — the predicate is False either way. Right input, wrong assertion, green test.

Also worth keeping: **a guard's behaviour can be correct by accident.** The `spawn*` launchers kept working only because `os.P_WAIT` is an `ast.Attribute` and failed an `isinstance(..., ast.Constant)` test; `os.spawnv(0, …)` was dark. And **latent is not safe** — every regression in this PR was unreachable in the tree today, which is exactly why nothing caught them.

#### The design question this PR should not have tried to answer

`_without_printed_text` is now a hand-rolled shell parser grown under review pressure: echo/printf, path-qualified verbs, redirection prefixes in both orders, `VAR=` assignments, recipe prefixes, quote tracking, clause terminators, nested command substitution, backticks, arithmetic. Each addition was individually correct and each enlarged the surface the next one could break. That, not carelessness, is why the rounds did not converge.

Its two consumers have **opposite risk profiles**, and they currently share one increasingly clever function:

* `_invocations` — the #24 wiring filter. A false positive here **silently unwires a stage** (a hint counts as an invocation and the wiring test stays green). Wants a conservative, tight positive rule.
* `stage_launch_offenders` — "nothing outside an orchestrator runs a stage". A false positive here is a visible red that someone fixes or allowlists. Can afford to be loose.

Splitting them, or replacing the hand-rolled scan with a real shell parser for the `_invocations` side, is the actual fix. Filing as its own piece of work rather than a 5th round.

#### Residuals, stated rather than left implicit

* the Makefile/workflow branch requires a `python`/`$PY` token, so a **directly-executed script** (`./foo/qc_gate.py`) is outside its scope — pre-existing at every commit, not changed here, and arguably wrong
* a **wrapper** (`die "…run qc_verdict.py…"`) is not an `echo` and is not removed
* a target **assembled at runtime** is invisible to any static check
* the negative-control `assert neutered != line` guards a future fixture row and is deliberately not mutation-covered — no row can trip it without also failing the main assertion

Co-Authored-By: Ziggy <ziggy@artificialhumanity.io>

### Deferred from #78 (four findings, left OPEN on the PR)

Owner called `13df79d` the last change to those two files, so the round that landed after it is recorded here rather than fixed. All four are captured on the PR as unresolved threads with replies; none is resolved, because none is fixed.

**MEDIUM — `_argv_printed_filter`'s two halves run on opposite premises.** The exemption test was corrected to treat element 0 of a `shell=True` list as a command line; the `survivors = None` two lines below still cites the retracted "a list argv is already split". Observable: byte-identical shell lines get opposite verdicts depending on whether they arrive via `os.system(...)` or `subprocess.run([...], shell=True)`. Not a regression — unchanged from `d2c6113` — but the docstring now contradicts itself. **The honest fix is the split above, not another special case:** element 0 of a `shell=True` list *is* a shell line and belongs on the string path entirely.

**Two LOWs that are both defects in MY MUTATION HARNESS, not in the code.** The behaviour is correct at every site; what is missing is a mutation that can see it. This is the third mechanism to add to the rule above, and the most mechanical:

* **A fix applied at N sites needs a mutation that hits all N.** M15 patches the substitution separator with `str.replace(old, new, 1)` — the *first* of two identical call sites. The backtick half is unpinned: revert it alone and the suite is green.
* **A shared constant is what makes one mutation cover N sites.** I hardcoded `(?![\w/.-])` inline in `_RECIPE_ECHO` instead of interpolating `_VERB_END`, so M13 — which mutates the `_VERB_END` binding — cannot reach it. Revert that one and the suite is green. (Janis also notes, correctly, that what `_VERB_END` buys in `_RECIPE_ECHO` is the `.`/`-` half, not the interior-`/` half — `_RECIPE_ECHO` has no path prefix.)

**LOW — a fixture that does not earn its line.** `("Makefile", "\tpython scripts/echo/qc_gate.py --apply")` duplicates the row above it; ` --apply` is inert for both conjuncts of the branch's append condition and for all four assertions. Worse than harmless: its comment presents it as the discriminating case, so a later cleanup will keep the duplicate and drop the real one. **Corollary to the rule: a fixture earns its line only if some mutation is red with it and green without** — which is a check that can be run mechanically over the fixture list, not just over the fixes.

Running total for this item, so the next person does not have to reconstruct it: a mutation battery is necessary and not sufficient; span the input space by breaking what the new rows have in common; make sure the assertion can see the defect; cover every site a fix touched; and hold fixtures to the same bar as fixes.
